title: Pool Tile Scale & Dark Waterline Band: How to Clean It
meta: Why pool tiles in Sanur turn white or dark at the waterline, what causes it, and practical steps to remove calcium scale and grout stains safely.
intro: That chalky ring or stubborn dark band along your pool tile is almost always a mix of evaporated minerals, algae film, and iron staining that builds up where the water level shifts day to day. In Sanur's salty air and hard PDAM or well water, it appears faster than you would expect. The good news: most of it comes off with the right cleaner, a soft brush, and a little patience – no acid blasting required.

paragraphs: Sanur sits metres from the Indian Ocean, so every surface carries a thin film of salt and humidity around the clock. Add tropical evaporation rates and a supply line fed by PDAM tap water or a rooftop tank drawing from a borehole, and you get a recipe for rapid mineral concentration on tile faces.

The dark band just below the waterline is usually three things layered together: calcium carbonate pulled out as water evaporates, a slimy biofilm of algae that thrives in the warm still zone, and trace iron oxide that leaches from old plumbing or well water. Older villas built in the 1990s are especially vulnerable because the original grout was often plain cement mixed without any penetrating sealer.

sections.h2: What to Use (and What to Avoid)
paragraphs: Start gentle. A soft-bristle nylon brush and warm soapy water will lift light film without scratching the glaze. For heavier deposits, mix one part white vinegar to four parts water and apply with a sponge. Let it sit five minutes, then scrub in small circles and rinse thoroughly before re-chlorinating.
For organic stains in the dark band, a paste of baking soda and a splash of water left on for ten minutes works well. Wipe off, rinse, and you are done.

One critical safety note: never combine an acid-based descaler with chlorine or any chlorine-containing product. The fumes released can cause serious respiratory damage. If you notice a sharp chemical smell while cleaning, stop immediately, open windows, step outside, and call a professional to finish the job safely.
bullets: Soft nylon brush – not wire wool, which etches ceramic glaze
White vinegar diluted 1:4 for mineral film
Baking-soda paste for algae and iron staining
Dedicated pH-2 pool descaler for thick calcium build-up
Never mix acids with chlorine products

sections.h2: Removing Calcium Scale Step by Step
paragraphs: That rough white ridge is calcium carbonate. In Sanur the dry season (roughly May through September) drives evaporation so hard that the band can thicken noticeably within two weeks if you do not intervene.
Work top to bottom so dissolved minerals wash away instead of re-depositing lower on the wall. Keep the tile wet throughout; dried descaler leaves its own residue.
bullets: Brush the area with a non-abrasive pad soaked in dilute vinegar or a commercial descaler (pH around 2).
Let it work for five to ten minutes – do not let it dry on the surface.
Scrub gently along the grout line in circular motions.
Rinse from the top down with clean hose water.
If a visible ridge remains, wait 24 hours and repeat once.
Avoid full-strength muriatic acid on old villa tiles; the glaze can craze and start absorbing moisture over time.

paragraphs: Vertical dark streaks running below the waterline are usually trapped algae and iron oxide that have worked their way into unsealed cement grout. In many older Sanur villas the original joints were never sealed, so they act like tiny sponges pulling in every mineral-rich splash.

Before you start, turn off circulation for about an hour so the area dries slightly. Apply a grout-safe cleaner or a paste of three-percent hydrogen peroxide directly onto the joint. Work with a small stiff brush held flat against the grout so the bristles do not drag across neighbouring tiles. Wipe with a damp cloth, rinse well, and let the joint dry completely before re-filling or re-chlorinating.

Once dry, apply a penetrating grout sealer. Re-seal every twelve months – ideally just before the rainy season kicks in around November – because constant humidity keeps joints damp and invites new staining.

sections.h2: Keeping It Clean Between Deep Cleans
paragraphs: A few small habits save hours of scrubbing later. Keep the water level steady; a line that bobs up and down leaves a fresh deposit band every single day. Top up from a filtered source rather than straight from a garden hose if your supply is noticeably hard.

Brush tile surfaces weekly, including the strip just above the waterline where evaporation concentrates minerals fastest. Maintain pH between 7.2 and 7.6: below that range calcium precipitates on walls, above it the water attacks grout and metal fittings.

After heavy rain in the wet season (November to March), give the waterline one extra check. Runoff carries iron and organic matter that settles quickly in still tropical air and starts staining within days.
bullets: Keep water level consistent; top up from a filtered source when possible
Brush tiles and the zone just above the waterline once a week
Hold pH at 7.2–7.6 to balance scale and corrosion
Inspect the waterline after each major storm
Re-seal grout annually, before the rainy season

faq.q: Can I use muriatic acid on my pool tiles?
faq.a: Only in heavily diluted form and with great care. On older Sanur villa tiles the glaze may already be micro-cracked, and full-strength acid will widen those cracks, letting moisture wick into the substrate. A pH-2 commercial descaler or dilute vinegar is safer and usually just as effective for the band you are seeing.

faq.q: Why does the dark band keep coming back even after I clean it?
faq.a: Most often it is because the water level fluctuates daily (evaporation plus topping up), so a new deposit line forms every day. Stabilise your level, brush that strip weekly, and make sure your pH is in range. If the stain returns within two weeks of a thorough clean, there may be an iron source in your well or supply line worth investigating.

faq.q: Is it safe to scrub the tile while chlorine is still in the water?
faq.a: Brushing with plain water or a mild soap solution is fine. What is not safe is mixing any acid-based cleaner (vinegar, descaler, muriatic acid) with residual chlorine – the reaction releases toxic gas. Drain or lower the water slightly below the area you are cleaning, work quickly, rinse thoroughly, and only re-chlorinate once all cleaning products have been washed away.
